Clip 01
8 TestFlight builds

Latitude — shooting Apple Log stills iOS doesn't allow

Apple Log preserves 2–3 stops more highlight and shadow than the standard pipeline — and Apple doesn't expose it through the stills API, because Log is a video-only colour space. So Latitude records a 300 ms ProRes clip on the shutter and pulls the best frame out of it. That clip is kept as the negative: every edit afterwards re-develops from 10-bit log source, not from an 8-bit JPEG. The look switcher on my portrait above is the same idea, running in your browser.

The core bet
ProRes 422 HQ in Apple Log (10-bit 4:2:2), ~9 frames at 30 fps, read back with AVAssetReader. The trade was accepted deliberately: video formats cap at 4K, so a CINE still is 8.3 MP against FILM's 12/48 MP. Every competitor applies looks on top of a conventional still instead.
Picking the frame
The first frame carries the jolt of the tap, so all frames are scored with a Tenengrad gradient metric — sparse grid, under 2 ms each — and the earliest frame within 0.90× of the best wins, so fast moments survive. The metric is pure and deterministic: capture and every later re-bake choose the same frame, so framing never jumps. Rewritten in two passes to cap peak memory at ~25 MB instead of ~220 MB.
Three render paths, one image
A Metal fragment shader drives the 30–60 fps viewfinder; Core Image bakes the capture; a third path re-bakes in the gallery. They have to agree byte-for-byte or the photo visibly changes when you open it — which made parity the architectural rule of the project, and the largest source of bugs in it.
The grain that looked like rain
Streaks at 41.8° and 92° — exactly the rotation angles of the noise octaves. Root cause: uint2(float2) on negative coordinates is undefined in Metal; Apple GPUs saturate to zero, freezing the hash along one axis. Converting to int2 first fixed it. The measurement of the angle is what cracked it.
Concurrency
Real-time capture, a main-actor UI and background inference sharing state under Swift 6 strict concurrency: @MainActor isolation with nonisolated(unsafe) mirror properties written only via didSet, so a torn read is always old-or-new — never incoherent.
Built, then cut
A Core ML depth-of-field pipeline (Depth Anything V2, live ANE inference at 8–15 Hz, bleed-free defocus) went through five iterations and was deleted — it still read as a blur vignette, which wasn't the product bar. Removing it cut 48 MB from the bundle.
Scale & status
~35,600 lines of Swift across 72 files, plus ~1,300 lines of Metal; 27 recipes; 84-field Codable metadata with legacy migrations. 8 TestFlight builds shipped to internal and external testers. Not on the App Store yet.

Alpha Club — a fitness platform with a physical layer

A fitness and community app with a tactical identity: GPS runs, workouts, daily missions, XP across a 20-rank progression, a social feed with stories and DMs, and a world map of members. The differentiator is physical: collectible challenge coins sold as real objects, validated and unlocked inside the app.

Physical ↔ digital
Coins ship from a Shopify store carrying single-use codes; members submit a photo, an admin back-office validates and issues a code, and the app plays a cinematic unwrap — 3D fragment assembly, ember particles and an SVG radial glow, built in Reanimated 4. Code stock is managed and reconciled in the back-office.
Server-authoritative, locked down
Supabase Postgres with RLS on every table restricted to authenticated, privileged operations behind SECURITY DEFINER RPCs gated by an admin check, profile columns locked by GRANTs and the admin flag protected by a trigger. 111 SQL migrations, 4 edge functions. The client renders; it never decides progression.
Tracking that survives
Run duration is derived from wall-clock rather than accumulated ticks, so it self-corrects after the OS suspends the app; state persists to disk and recovers after a hard kill.
Compliance as a design problem
Dropped ACCESS_BACKGROUND_LOCATION on Android while keeping background tracking through a foreground service — sidestepping Google Play's heaviest review path without losing the feature.
Stack
React Native 0.81 · Expo SDK 54 · New Architecture + Hermes · TypeScript · Reanimated 4 · NativeWind · MapLibre · Zustand + TanStack Query · HealthKit and Health Connect · EAS Build with OTA updates · ~35 feature-first modules.
Status
v1.0.0 production builds complete on EAS for both platforms, tested externally, pending store submission.

Clip 03
In production · v12.40

Prozis Studio — the pipeline, turned into a tool

I coordinate the AI product-photography project for Prozis, a sportswear brand — and when the manual workflow stopped scaling, I built the tool that runs it. A desktop app that drives the whole pipeline against a live generation API: plan, generate, correct, upscale, reframe — for a team that never opens a terminal. Forty-plus releases deep, in daily production use.

API orchestration
Python backend driving the Magnific API (Seedream 5 Pro Edit, Nano Banana Pro, Flux, Ideogram): parallel dispatch behind a shared semaphore with staggered starts to respect the rate limits, task polling, and a hard prompt-budget guard — the API rejects anything over 4096 characters, so prompts are built inside the budget rather than truncated at send.
Computer vision, on-device
The client's constraint was zero paid APIs beyond the one provider — and that provider has no vision or segmentation endpoint. So all of it runs locally and free: SegFormer segmentation, mask union, and a harmonic membrane fusion (∇²F = 0, solved with Gauss–Seidel SOR) plus per-channel CDF histogram matching to close the seam between generated and photographed pixels.
A generator as a measuring instrument
To locate a garment with no detection endpoint available, the tool asks the cheapest model to paint it in a marker colour — auto-picked as whichever hue is least present in the source — then reads which pixels lit up. The painted image is discarded inside the function: what comes out is a bounding box, never pixels.
Test discipline
Around 60 suites, all green, run against the packaged artifact rather than the working folder. The whole run executes in demo mode behind a network listener asserting that not one call reaches the paid API — full coverage at zero credits.
Autonomy, with an approved ceiling
The agent simulates the cost, announces it in plain words and waits for one yes. Inside that budget it runs without interrupting: generate, then look at the result beside the real garment — logo orientation, drawstrings, collar, seams, colour, drape — write the verdict in concrete words, fold the named defect into the next prompt, repeat. At the ceiling it stops, even mid-run. Nothing is applied automatically; the final call is always a human's. This is the shape I believe autonomy should take: free inside a boundary a person drew.
Designed for failure, not just success
Once the API returns a URL the generation is already paid for — so failing to fetch it is never an outcome. Three retries with growing waits, and if it still doesn't arrive the link is kept and flagged rather than discarded. The live job table, the upscale queue and the review flow are all built on the same principle: never silently lose work a human is waiting on.
Built for non-engineers
Single-file desktop app, double-click to run, two themes. Every design call driven by real production feedback from the person using it daily.
Shipped iteratively
v8.0 → v12.40 in production use — each release closing a gap the previous one exposed, from a signed-int32 seed bug to a colour cast that turned out to be my own correction decaying to zero far from the seam.

Clip 04
v1.49 · customer-facing

Prozis Try-On — a fitting room that had to survive the real store

A mobile PWA where a customer picks garments, sends a few photos and their height, and one tap returns them wearing the clothes. Two ways in: the app itself, or a button living inside a Prozis product page. Every hard decision in it came from a constraint I hit rather than a preference I had.

The discovery that chose the architecture
prozis.com answers 410 to any read from outside a browser, and builds its gallery in JavaScript after the first request — a server-side scraper reads an empty shell, when it isn't shown the door. So the reader is the button, running inside the customer's own browser: JSON-LD → og: → DOM, thumbnails shrunk to 512 px in canvas before they travel. No CORS, no bot-blocking, no banned IP, nothing to break when the template changes.
A code a human can read aloud
Garments cross from the store to the app as a six-letter basket code drawn from a confusion-free alphabet — no O/0, I/1, L, S/5, B/8, Z/2, G/6. Open routes stay open (whoever pressed the button is already on the site and can't have a code yet); anything that spends money stays locked, behind a daily ceiling and a domain allowlist.
Read the product once, for everybody
Each product sheet is classified a single time — category, English keyword, and per photo whether it is front / back / side / detail and whether it is useful at all (size charts and packaging go in the bin). Cached for 30 days. The scene's own orientation then drives the references: a back view asks for back photos, back base, back scene, in that order.
Degrading where the platform is poorer
Inside a native WebView there is no camera API, no share sheet, no downloads folder. Each one falls to a working path — the native camera through a file field with capture, then the next step, then "hold your finger on the image" — instead of hanging. Detection first, then a route down; the same code in a browser and in the app, without ifs scattered everywhere.
Privacy as a build rule
Photos, prompts and names are never stored. Keys live only on the server. The store button touches no cart, no account, no cookie — it keeps one key in local storage and nothing else.
Test discipline
173 automated tests — 112 browser, 39 server, 22 end-to-end from product page through basket to a dressed app — run against clean extraction, at zero credits spent.

Clip 05
v0.7 · in build

Prozis Atelier — giving the agent hands, and giving the human doubt

A platform that turns reference photographs into a technical garment spec, then drives CLO3D itself — clean, open, simulate, measure, portrait, export GLB. The interesting problem was never the automation. It was making sure the specialist can always see how much the machine actually knew.

The agent decides; the platform refuses
There is no photo → pattern feature in CLO3D — confirmed twice by CLO themselves — so the reading is the agent's job. It measures the garment against the mannequin and writes the entire 2D plan: panels, seams, prints. A verifier then checks that plan before a single command reaches the 3D tool — crossed outlines, points 0.22 mm apart, seam pairs 99% mismatched, a print on a panel that doesn't exist — and predicts the finished height. Given a deliberately broken plan it caught all seven faults. The platform decides nothing for the agent; it only refuses what cannot work.
Then it executes, end to end
Draw, sew confirming every seam one by one, glue the prints onto the flat pattern so the simulation curves them the way real fabric does, hang, drape, simulate, measure, export GLB — 24 order types, no human touching the 3D tool.
Read / calculated / estimated
Every field of the generated spec carries its own provenance label, so a measurement lifted from the reference never looks like one the model guessed. Unmarked AI output invites misplaced trust — the confidence marker is the feature, not a footnote.
The work never leaves the machine
Photographs, .zprj, .glb and .dxf files stay in a folder the user picks at start-up, reached from the browser through the File System Access API. The cloud holds only access codes and keys — nothing of the work itself. Chrome or Edge required, deliberately.
A folder as the bridge
The browser writes orders as JSON; a Python arm dropped inside CLO3D reads them, executes and writes results back — 24 order types, reinstalled on every start so it can never drift out of date. It solved the plugin problem without a line of C++.
A base sock you can pull
A fully customisable knitted base — 24/7 crew, size 39/41, 200 needles — split into nine structural zones (cuff, leg, logo, instep, heel, arch, sole, toe), each carrying its own knit structure and its own stretch limit. The knit is real geometry, loop by loop, so you can grab the toe and pull it to 10× and watch the panel tell you the fabric has stopped. Every product variant starts from this one.
Access, per person
Individual codes that can be paused or regenerated one at a time, and a back office that is separate by design — no door to it from inside the platform.
